title: Remarks at Harrisburg, Pa
paragraphs: The President of the Senate said:

Mr. President, representing the Senate I desire to express our regret that we cannot escort you to our capitol; but there is significance and sentiment in the fact that we can come here in the shadow of that old church where was nominated the first Harrison. We wish to express to you our greeting for the labor interests of Pennsylvania, and to assure you that we are resting very happy and contented, and hope that the happiness and prosperity which has so long blessed land will continue.
The Speaker of the Lower House of the Pennsylvania Legislature said:

Mr. President: I have the honor to present to you the members of the lower house of [?] legislation of Pennsylvania. We adjourned under a resolution to assemble [?] here upon the arrival of this train to greet you and to wish you godspeed [?] on your journey and a safe return to your home. We regret, sir, exceedingly, [?] that time would not permit us to pass [?] a resolution requesting your presence in the House to-day, your honor, [?] [illegible] but in the absence of that we have done [?] that which we thought was best under the [?] [illegible] circumstances; we come down to be present and greet you in this way. [?] (Applause.)
Congressman, Mr. Speaker, Mr. President, and Mr. Mayor, and Gentlemen and Ladies:

I am very greatly touched and pleased by this greeting- a wholly unexpected one. I had not supposed that my speech-making would begin before to-morrow. There is not much for me to say to you. I feel rather when I come here, like sitting at the feet of Gamaliel and learning. (Laughter.)

The prosperity in which you of this state, you of this city, have so abundantly shared must come primarily from two sources, the individual skill and efficiency of the individual man, capitalist or wage worker, working for himself as a foundation, but with upon it the super-structure of the men who, working not merely for themselves but for one another. (Cheers and applause)

The President of the Senate was kind enough to speak of what has been done for the wage worker, and therefore the citizens as a whole, in this State. I go away from Washington with a light heart, very largely because of the admirable work done by the gentlemen on [?] the Anthracite Strike Commission. (Applause.) And surely no publication by any association designed purely to teach a moral lesson to our people can be better worth scanning and learning than the document containing the conclusions of those men; and if as a people we will take to heart [?] the lessons taught therein, it will be the better for all of us. [?]

Fundamentally our interests are the same. Fundamentally you hurt or help some of our people and inevitably you hurt or help others. Fundamentally the most important lesson to be learned in our national life is the lesson of our solidarity of interests, and that [?] every man of us, if he is fit to be a citizen of this republic, must pull his own weight, and must also do his best to help his brother at the same time. (Cheers and applause.)

Both pages are on frame 0005 (left half folio 1, right half folio 2 with typed "-2-"), as listed. The pencilled "4" at the upper left of folio 2 is not transcribed. The document includes the remarks of the President of the Pennsylvania Senate and of the Speaker of the House before Roosevelt's reply; they are transcribed as typed. The lower part of folio 1 (the Speaker's remarks and the line "The President said:") is heavily smudged or blotted across most lines; the words are not struck through with a pen but are partly obscured, so obscured stretches are given as uncertain readings. Folio 1: two typed lines after "contented," are struck through by hand and mostly illegible; "and hope that the" is written above them and "will continue" after "land". The word before "land" is overtyped or blotted. Folio 2: about ten typed lines after "interests," are struck through by hand with heavy wavy lines; only scattered words show through. The small handwritten addition above "interests," reads doubtfully as "and that". "will take to heart" and "all of us." are partly smudged. The "E" of "Every" is overwritten by hand with a small "e". "workingfor" is typed as one word with a hand mark separating it; "oursolidarity" likewise has a hand mark between "our" and "solidarity". Many letters are overtyped (e.g. "surely", "teach", "admirable", "inevitably", "learned"); final readings given. Third look: "on": the vowel of the word before "the Anthracite" is an "o" and an "i" typed over each other, so "on" and "in" cannot be told apart. After "your honor," one stray typed character under the smudge is not legible.
